title: The Grateful Tartaro and the Heren-Suge
subtitle: A ball-game bargain frees a prisoner

learningObjectives.text: What does the Tartaro ask for in exchange for the ball?
How does the boy get the stable key?

ball.author: Basque storytellers; collected and translated by Wentworth Webster
ball.translator: Wentworth Webster, with assistance from Julien Vinson and other local contributors
ball.locator: THE GRATEFUL TARTARO AND THE HEREN-SUGE.; THE GRATEFUL TARTARO AND THE HEREN-SUGE., normalized characters 480-1491
ball.excerpt: The next day the two sons of the king were playing at ball against (the wall of) the stable where the Tartaro was confined, and the ball went into the stable. One of the boys goes and asks the Tartaro-- "Throw me back my ball, I beg you." He says to him, "Yes, if you will deliver me." He replies, "Yes, yes," and he threw him the ball. A moment after, the ball goes again to the Tartaro. He asks for it again; and the Tartaro says: "If you will deliver me, I will give it you." The boy says, "Yes, yes," takes his ball, and goes off. The ball goes there for the third time, but the Tartaro will not give it before he is let out. The boy says that he has not the key. The Tartaro says to him: "Go to your mother, and tell her to look in your right ear, because something hurts you there. Your mother will have the key in her left pocket, and take it out." The boy goes, and does as the Tartaro had told him. He takes the key from his mother, and delivers the Tartaro. When he was letting him go, he said to him:
ball.note: Verbatim English text from Webster's second edition, collected chiefly in Labourd. The collection distinguishes local tales from French-derived contes des fées and compares some motifs with wider European stories.

narrativeBlocks.title: A ball enters the stable
narrativeBlocks.body: A king keeps a Tartaro in a stable. When a boy's ball rolls inside, the prisoner offers to return it if the boy will free him.

narrativeBlocks.title: The boy takes the key
narrativeBlocks.body: The Tartaro tells the boy how to take the key from his mother. He escapes and promises to help later.

narrativeBlocks.title: A Basque collection with cross-tradition parallels
narrativeBlocks.body: Webster places this story among Basque Tartaro and serpent legends, while noting that the Heren-Suge cycle resembles wider European dragon-slayer motifs. Keep the local telling and the comparison distinct.

narrativeBlocks.title: A small bargain launches the plot
narrativeBlocks.body: The returned ball is not a harmless ending: the boy's promise frees the Tartaro and creates a future debt.
